title: They differ
hookLine: rebirth, resurrection, return, nothing, mystery: kept apart, each in its home
carry: each stays in its own home

cards: Five doors in one hallway, each with a different name on it. Behind one, a life comes back in a new body. Behind another, the dead are raised.
Behind the third, the spirit goes back to where it came from. The fourth opens onto nothing at all. The fifth won't open, and the people who built it say that is the honest answer.
For weeks this block has visited each door. Today, look at all five from the hallway, and knock down no walls between them.

teach.b: First, rebirth. Buddhists teach rebirth shaped by karma, without a fixed soul passing from life to life.
The Bhagavad Gita gives a Hindu picture: as a person casts off worn clothes and puts on new ones, the self casts off worn bodies. Two homes, two vocabularies, and they don't say the same thing.
Second, resurrection. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Martha, "I am the resurrection, and the life." Christians hope for the raising of the dead.
The Qur'an says every soul shall taste death, and speaks of a Day of Resurrection when each soul is paid what it earned.
Third, return. Ecclesiastes says, "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it."
At Sikh funerals the bedtime prayer, Kirtan Sohila, is sung, and death is spoken of as going home.
Fourth, nothing, or mystery. Lucretius taught that the ages after death will trouble us no more than the ages before birth. Socrates kept two options open: dreamless sleep, or a journey.
Confucius, asked about death, turned the question back to life.
So the block lands here: they differ. This path doesn't read a Buddhist teacher and a Christian priest as two versions of one answer.
Each answer lives inside a whole way of life, with its own texts, rites and hopes, and pulled out and blended, it loses what makes it make sense. So each stays in its own home, and anyone can visit.

how: Traditions teach different things about death: Buddhists and Hindus speak of rebirth in their own distinct ways, Christians and Muslims of resurrection and judgment, Sikhs of going home, and some philosophers of nothing at all. Interfaith settings often let each speak for itself.

games.q: a friend says every tradition really believes the same thing about death, just in different words. what does today's lesson say?
o: they agree underneath, in different words.
they differ, and each answer belongs to its own way of life.
only one of them deserves to be taken seriously.
games.why: they differ. each answer lives inside its own texts, rites and hopes, and loses its sense when it's blended with the others.

practice: On this block's first day, the invitation was to write what you think; now write a few lines again: what do you think happens at death, or what do you honestly not know?
Use your own words, not a borrowed sentence, unless that sentence really is yours. If you kept that first page, the two can sit side by side later, with no grade for either.

wordCard.voice: They differ. Rebirth, resurrection, return, nothing, mystery: real answers from real traditions, each kept in its own home, never blended into one. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: each stays in its own home. Each answer makes sense where it lives. Day eight hundred seventeen, done.
